It's worth checking the figure-related comments against the PDF, especially the BD3-LM superscripts and Fig. 9. Since ICLR's reviewer AI policy is printed on every page, please rework this into your own words and judgement before submitting.

# ICLR 2027 Review: UnAct (Gradient-Free Unlearning via Targeted Activation Intervention)

I read pages 1–20: the main text and Appendices A–I. Appendices J–N (class-selectivity, timing, ViT details, relearning, coverage bound) I did not read in full, so I judged them only by how the main text describes them.

---

## Summary

The paper proposes **UnAct**, a post-hoc method that removes a whole class from a trained classifier using only forward passes over a few images of that class. It does not use labels, gradients or retained data. Each round, it scores the units in a few late layers. On ResNet-18 the score is the channel's mean post-ReLU activation. On ViT-B/16 it is a direct logit attribution to a pseudo-labelled class. It then picks the units above the p-th percentile and multiplies their incoming and outgoing weights by γ < 1. This repeats for k rounds, re-scoring each time. Because selection is by rank, the size of the edit is bounded by p and k regardless of how many forget images there are or how the scores are scaled.

The main baselines are SSD and LFSSD. Experiments use ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-20 and CIFAR-100, plus ViT-B/16 on CIFAR-10. Findings:
- **Full forget set:** UnAct is competitive with the baselines on ResNet-18, with Δ to retraining of 0.08, 0.80 and 1.15.
- **Few forget images:** SSD and LFSSD can collapse retain accuracy; UnAct stays within 2.45 points of retraining, and with five images Δ is about 0.2–1.4.
- **ViT:** UnAct's Δ is 11.5 against SSD's 33.7.

The paper also reports, to its credit, that a trivial logit mask matches every method on Δ. It also reports that a linear probe still recovers the forget class (AUROC ≥ 0.98) after every method, including UnAct.

## Strengths

1. **Simple, cheap and data-light.** The method needs only forward passes over the forget images. It needs no labels (bit-identical results with labels replaced, App. B), no training-set statistics and no optimization. That is a meaningful practical gain over SSD and LFSSD, which need a pass over the whole training set to compute importance (1,248 s on ViT).
2. **The rank-based bound is a clean design idea.** Fixing the edit size through (p, k) rather than through a threshold on a ratio explains the robustness at small n. The diagonal structure in the (p, k) grid (Fig. 3c, Table 5) supports the coverage argument.
3. **Unusually honest evaluation.** The paper:
   - compares against a trivial logit-mask baseline;
   - runs a linear probe on the penultimate features;
   - measures agreement with the retrained model's predictions (Agr_f);
   - reports relearning;
   - re-selects SSD's α at every n with an oracle (Table 11);
   - checks held-out classes on which SSD's own paper reports failures;
   - tests a selection rule that needs no retrained model (Table 6).

   This calibration of what Δ does and does not certify is a contribution in itself.
4. **Thorough reporting.** Full hyperparameter grids, per-class spreads and released code make the claims easy to check.

## Weaknesses

1. **Significance is undercut by the paper's own controls.** A logit mask that zeroes one classifier row reaches Δ = 0.09, 0.25 and 0.33, which matches or beats UnAct on CIFAR-20 and CIFAR-100. It needs no images at all and is unaffected by n. The probe recovers the class with AUROC ≥ 0.98 after UnAct, and relearning is fast. So within the class-unlearning setting studied here, it is unclear what UnAct gives a practitioner that the logit mask does not. The "few images" regime, which is the paper's headline advantage, is exactly where the trivial baseline also works perfectly.

   The authors need to state a threat model or use case in which UnAct beats the logit mask, for example:
   - an attacker with white-box access to weights or features;
   - a sub-class or instance-level forget set;
   - forgetting where the class identity is unknown.

   Without that, the method's improvement over SSD at small n fixes a failure of SSD rather than showing progress on unlearning.

2. **Agreement with retraining is worse than the baselines'.** Table 9 shows UnAct sends forgotten images to the same class as the retrained model only 31.4% of the time, against about 62–65% for SSD, LFSSD and the logit mask. The pattern repeats on CIFAR-20 and CIFAR-100. This is a substantive point against UnAct's fidelity to retraining, but it appears only in the appendix. It belongs in the main text and should be discussed alongside Δ.

3. **Narrow empirical scope.**
   - Only CIFAR-scale data.
   - One CNN, plus a "preliminary" ViT on which UnAct still loses 6.5 retain points relative to retraining.
   - One training seed.
   - Class-level forgetting only, one class per request.

   No ImageNet-scale experiment, no other architectures (e.g., WideResNet, ConvNeXt) and no instance or sub-class forgetting are included. This limits how general the claims can be. The score also has to be redesigned per architecture (activation for CNNs, logit attribution with a pseudo-label for ViTs). That weakens the "any architecture with a classifier head" framing in §3.2.

4. **Limited baselines.** Only SSD and LFSSD are compared. Several methods the paper itself cites also work from forget samples only, without retained data:
   - Boundary Unlearning;
   - JiT;
   - unit-pruning approaches (Wang et al. 2022; Pochinkov & Schoots 2024), which are the closest methodological relatives.

   At least the closest of these, adapted to the forget-only setting, should be included. The excluded methods use more information, but showing where UnAct sits on the cost/quality frontier would still help. An "activation pruning with zeroing, one shot" ablation would also isolate the contribution of iteration and soft attenuation in the main text.

5. **Model selection on the test split.** All operating points, for every method, are picked by Δ on test accuracy. The authors acknowledge this, and it applies equally to all methods. Still, at differences of about 0.1–1 Δ point (Table 2) with five classes and one seed, many full-class comparisons are within noise; Table 8's standard deviations are of similar size. Claims such as "closest on CIFAR-10" should be softened, or supported with a held-out validation split and several seeds.

6. **Weak motivation for the few-image regime in class unlearning.** If the entire class must be removed, why would the requester have only five images? The model owner usually holds the training data. The scenario seems better suited to cases where the class's training data has already been deleted. That case should be stated, and its interaction with the GDPR-style motivation in the introduction clarified.

7. **Incremental novelty.** Scoring units by activation on the target class and suppressing them is close to prior unit-level removal work (Bau et al. 2020; Pochinkov & Schoots 2024; Wang et al. 2022). The new elements are rank-bounded iterative soft attenuation and requiring no retained data. These are sensible but modest. The coverage bound (a union bound) is elementary.

8. **Presentation.** The text is dense and number-heavy. Many key results are pushed to Appendices G–N, among them the Agr_f finding, the relearning results, the ViT details and the sequential-request results. The abstract leans on ratios such as "19× faster" and "430× closer" that are computed relative to collapsed baselines; these magnify small absolute differences.

## Questions for the authors

1. Under what concrete threat model or deployment scenario is UnAct preferable to the zero-cost logit mask? Can you show a metric on which UnAct clearly beats it?
2. Agr_f is far below the baselines'. Does this mean UnAct's edited model is further from retraining than SSD's in a meaningful sense? Would a distribution-level metric such as KL to the retrained model's outputs on forget images change the ranking?
3. How does UnAct behave with sub-class or random-sample forgetting, where activation scoring cannot rely on class-selective units?
4. Can you report results over several training seeds, with a held-out validation split for operating-point selection?
5. How does UnAct compare with Boundary Unlearning, JiT, or one-shot activation pruning (zeroing the top units) under the same forget-only access?
6. On ViT, retain accuracy stays 6.5 points below retraining. Does this gap shrink with larger scopes or different γ, or is it intrinsic to editing MLP neurons that feed the shared residual stream?
7. Does the score transfer to ImageNet-scale models with 1,000 classes, where late-layer units are less class-specific?

## Minor comments

- Table 1 lists LFSSD's limitation only as "approximate method", yet the paper shows it collapses at small n. Make this consistent.
- Several tables mix A10 and L4 evaluations. This is noted, but it is distracting; please re-run everything on one device.
- In §3.3, the ViT pseudo-label "assumes a single-class forget set". State this restriction prominently in the problem formulation.
- The parameter fractions modified by UnAct (4.8% against 0.1–3.6%) should be discussed in the main text, since "targeted" is part of the title.

## Ratings

- **Soundness:** 3 / 4. The experiments are careful and honest within their scope, but use a single seed and test-split selection.
- **Presentation:** 2 / 4. The writing is dense, and important findings are left in the appendix.
- **Contribution:** 2 / 4.
- **Overall rating:** **4: marginally below the acceptance threshold**
- **Confidence:** 4: confident, but not absolutely certain.

**Justification.** UnAct is a simple, well-engineered, forward-only method, and its robustness when forget data is scarce is shown convincingly against SSD and LFSSD. The paper is also commendably transparent about the limits of its metric. That same transparency shows a trivial logit mask matching all methods on Δ, the class fully recoverable from the features, and UnAct agreeing with retraining less often than the baselines do. Together with the small scale, few baselines and single seed, this leaves the practical significance unclear. A stronger case for when UnAct beats trivial output-level suppression, plus broader experiments, would move this toward acceptance.

# Review: WorldAuditBench: Interactive 3D World Auditing with Multimodal Agents

## Summary

The paper introduces WorldAuditBench, a benchmark for "world auditing": an agent explores an interactive 3D environment and reports an anomaly that someone has planted in it. The benchmark has 213 hand-built, single-anomaly tasks across 13 environments (7 in Unreal Engine 5 with 126 tasks, 6 in Three.js with 87 tasks). The anomalies are grouped into 5 families with 15 categories: static physics, interactive physics, spatial consistency, temporal consistency and semantic consistency. Each task was accepted only after at least two independent human validators rated it Pass.

The paper compares two setups:
- **VLM-only agents.** One model acts and reasons in a closed loop, with a 40-action budget and memory and reporting tools exposed over MCP.
- **VLA–VLM pipeline.** Open-P2P 1.2B explores for 60 seconds, then a VLM analyses the fixed trajectory afterwards.

Five frontier models are tested, each run inside its own vendor's CLI harness. A GPT-6 Astra judge scores reports against a rubric. VLM-only agents reach 28–42% SR (excluding the two weakest models), VLA–VLM pipelines reach 6.6–17.4%, and humans reach 83.4%. Ablations cover starting distance, exploration budget, task guidance and multiple anomalies per scene, plus an exposure-versus-identification analysis.

## Strengths

1. **Well-motivated problem.** Many anomalies only show up through interaction, revisiting a place, or changing viewpoint (missing collision, disappearing objects, view-dependent visibility). Offline glitch benchmarks such as GlitchBench, VideoGameQA-Bench and VideoGlitchBench cannot test these. Table 1 places the work clearly against prior benchmarks.
2. **Clear taxonomy.** It draws on the game-bug literature (Lewis et al.; Truelove et al.; Butt et al.) and is organised by the kind of evidence needed to detect each anomaly, which fits the paper's thesis that action and reasoning are coupled.
3. **Careful task construction.** Every task is hand-crafted and accepted only after two independent Pass ratings on the same configuration; any change to the rubric triggers re-validation. Scenes are varied: indoor, urban, historical, industrial, natural and underwater.
4. **Useful analyses.** The split between exposure and identification (Section 6.3, with both geometric and human-rated exposure) is a good diagnostic. The guidance ablation shows that removing the anomaly-type hint costs about 17.5 pp, which suggests the benchmark mostly tests directed search.
5. **Practical reporting.** Cost and wall-clock time are reported, the licenses are documented, and the judge prompt includes defences against prompt injection.

## Weaknesses

1. **The headline "VLM-only beats VLA–VLM" result is confounded by engine and explorer.** Table 9 (Appendix D) shows the gap almost entirely on Unreal:

   | Engine | VLM-only SR | VLA–VLM SR |
   |---|---|---|
   | Unreal Engine 5 | 27.8–47.6% | 2.4–5.6% |
   | Three.js | 28.7–34.5% | 32.2–34.5% |

   On Three.js, Claude Opus 5 and Gemini 3.8 Flash do *as well or better* under VLA–VLM than as VLM agents. A likely explanation is that Open-P2P, a single small game-playing policy, does poorly in large UE5 regions. That is a statement about one VLA, not about coupling action with reasoning. The main text and abstract present the gap as a general property of the two paradigms; it should instead be stated per engine. Testing a second explorer would help separate the two effects, for example a scripted frontier or coverage explorer, or the VLM itself replaying a non-adaptive path.

2. **The budgets differ between paradigms.** VLM agents get 40 discrete actions, each moving up to 4 m or turning up to 180°, and intermediate frames can be inspected. The VLA gets 60 s sampled at 2 Hz. The paper says the budgets differ but never matches them, so we cannot tell whether the gap comes from adaptivity or from coverage. Geometric coverage is 91.1% versus 47.4%, which suggests the VLM-only agent simply covers more ground. A coverage-matched or distance-matched comparison is needed.

3. **The evaluation protocol rewards over-reporting.** Judge rule 2 says "other reports do not cancel a valid target finding", and the agents are told to use the full budget. An agent can therefore report many suspected bugs at no cost. The paper gives no precision or false-positive measure, yet the task statement itself stresses telling real defects from unusual but valid content. Please report the number of reports per task, the false-positive rate, or a precision-aware score. Appendix F already shows false-positive cases.

4. **The judge is not validated well enough.**
   - Agreement with humans (91.7%, κ=0.645) was measured only on *human* baseline reports, not on model reports, whose style, length and number of claims differ.
   - κ≈0.64 is moderate. With a few-point spread among the stronger models, the judge's noise could change the rankings.
   - The judge is GPT-6 Astra, which is also the top-ranked auditor. Self-preference bias should be ruled out, either by validating the judge on model reports or by repeating the evaluation with a judge from another family.

5. **Results are not statistically rigorous.** Each configuration appears to be run once, with no confidence intervals or repeated seeds. Many per-cell sample sizes are small:
   - semantic consistency in Three.js has n=2, giving 0% or 100% entries;
   - temporal consistency in Three.js has n=14;
   - the multi-anomaly study uses 42 runs per condition.

   Several ablation effects are within 1–2 tasks (+1.6 pp ≈ 2/126). Examples include the 1.5× budget, the "Near" condition for VLA–VLM, and dropping ICL. The text reads these as trends. Bootstrap CIs and at least 3 runs for the main table are needed.

6. **Models are confounded with harnesses.** Each model runs in a different agent CLI (Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Qwen Code), each with its own context management, system prompts and image handling. The paper admits that each comparison measures a model together with its harness, but the leaderboard is presented as a comparison of models. A single shared harness for all models, even as a secondary result, would make the rankings much easier to interpret.

7. **The memory claim is not supported.** The introduction says the memory tool "substantially improves anomaly discovery", but I found no ablation that removes the memory tools. Section 6.3 only compares VLM-only with VLA–VLM on exposed tasks, which changes many variables at once. Either add a no-memory ablation or soften the claim.

8. **The human baseline is under-specified.**
   - About 10 CS PhD students took part. Were any of them also task constructors or validators? Validators saw the rubrics.
   - Humans had 10 minutes of continuous control with no action cap, which is not comparable to 40 discrete actions.
   - Because of this, the 83.4% figure mixes perceptual skill with differences in budget and interface. Please report inter-participant agreement and how many actions or how much distance humans actually used.

9. **The scope is narrower than the framing.** Agents are always told the anomaly *type*, there is exactly one target per task, and the scenes are bounded. This is closer to directed search for a known kind of defect than to open-ended world auditing. The no-hint condition (15.9%) is arguably the realistic setting and deserves more attention, ideally on all models. The benchmark size (213 tasks; 7 UE environments split into 21 regions) is also modest for a benchmark paper.

10. **Release and reproducibility.** The UE5 environments come from Fab packages, which will be released only as runnable binaries. Some Unreal tasks are streamed from a remote runtime. Please state how long-term access will be guaranteed and whether third parties will be able to add new tasks.

## Questions for the authors

1. Can you explain the Three.js versus Unreal reversal in Table 9? Does the VLM-only advantage hold on Three.js at all?
2. How many reports do agents submit per task on average? What is the SR if more than k reports, or any confirmed false positive, counts as failure?
3. What is the judge's agreement with humans on *model* reports, and does it differ by auditor (especially GPT-6 Astra)?
4. What is the run-to-run variance of the main results?
5. What happens with a no-memory ablation, and with a shared harness for all models?
6. Were any human-baseline participants involved in task construction or validation?
7. In Section 6.3, are the "covered by both" subsets identical across paradigms? For the human-rated exposure subset, how many tasks are in each?

## Minor issues

- The Section 6.1 ablations use only Gemini 3.8 Flash on the Unreal subset. Please state clearly that the default numbers (33.3% / 5.6%) differ from Table 2's pooled numbers for this reason.
- Typo: "thein-context example" in Section 6.1.
- In Figure 4, the Muse and Qwen VLA times look larger than the VLM times. Please explain or clarify.
- The Table 7 caption and the surrounding text are interleaved in a way that makes them hard to read.
- The geometric coverage thresholds (7–16 m, ±41.4°) look arbitrary. Please justify them or report how sensitive the coverage numbers are to them.

## Overall assessment

The problem is timely and the benchmark is carefully built, with real value for testing interactive, evidence-seeking agents. However, the paper's main scientific claim — that coupling visual reasoning with action is what produces the performance gap — is undermined by several problems: a single weak VLA explorer, unmatched budgets, and a reversal on Three.js that only appears in the appendix. The evaluation also lacks a precision metric, variance estimates, judge validation on model outputs and a memory ablation. These problems can be fixed, but they are central to the paper's claims.

**Rating:** 4 (marginally below the acceptance threshold)
**Confidence:** 4
**Soundness:** 2 · **Presentation:** 3 · **Contribution:** 3

I would be inclined to raise my score if the authors reframe the paradigm comparison per engine, add a matched or alternative explorer baseline, report false positives and confidence intervals, and validate the judge on model reports.

# Review: GC-NCE — Graph-Constrained Nuisance-Aware Clinical Evidence Bottleneck for Medical Image Classification under Domain Shift

## Summary

The paper aims to make concept bottleneck models (CBMs) more robust under confounded domain shift in medical imaging. It identifies two problems: (i) an unconstrained diagnostic head weights concepts by source-domain correlations instead of their clinical roles, and (ii) concept scores leak nuisance information. To address them:

1. **Graph construction.** Four LLM agents (GPT-5.5) build typed per-class "clinical evidence graphs" from PubMed abstracts, with a deterministic compiler and a cross-agent negotiation round. The graphs contain diagnosis, mechanism, finding, anatomy and nuisance nodes, and each finding or mechanism has a role: direct, differential or related.
2. **Observability-aware refinement.** Concepts are posed as yes/no questions, labelled by an LLM on reports, and fit with logistic-regression readers on frozen WhyXrayCLIP / WhyLesionCLIP features. Readers with too little label support or validation AUROC below 0.65 are rewritten or replaced.
3. **Graph-constrained inference.** Finding scores are inferred through a noisy-OR mechanism model with anatomical-visibility temperatures. Diagnosis scores combine noisy-OR support (direct findings, target mechanisms) with multiplicative inhibition (differential evidence), averaged over the mechanism posterior.
4. **Adaptive nuisance correction.** A linear, cross-fitted, anatomy-residualized correction is applied along nuisance→finding edges. Whether to use it is decided per dataset from worst-group accuracy on source validation.

On the ten confounded benchmarks of Yang et al. (2024b, KnoBo), GC-NCE reports mean OOD AUROC of 78.5% (chest X-ray) and 84.5% (skin lesion). The strongest baselines reach 57.2% (KnoBo) and 79.2% (LaBo).

## Strengths

- **Well-motivated problem.** Concept names do not stop the diagnostic head from using shortcuts, and the paper argues this clearly. Fig. 1(b) shows concept–label correlations flipping sign between source and target, which makes the point concrete.
- **Principled structured head.** Separating support, differential inhibition, anatomy gating and nuisance edges is clinically sensible and builds on QMR-DT-style noisy-OR diagnostic networks. Constraining weights to [0,1] so differential evidence can never act as support is a clean inductive bias.
- **Large gains on the hardest chest X-ray splits.** NIH-pos rises from 38.6 to 77.0 and NIH-CheXpert from 51.0 to 85.9, with much smaller ID–OOD gaps.
- **Ablations go beyond removing components:**
  - Swapping the direct and differential roles costs 7.3 points (X-ray) and 19.9 points (skin).
  - Permuting which reader is assigned to which finding node costs 8.7 and 17.4 points.
  - Together these suggest the graph's *content* matters, not just the parametric form.
- **Careful nuisance-correction protocol.** It uses cross-fitting, anatomy residualization and target-free selection. Table 13 is candid that correction hurts on several datasets (ISIC-site −7.0).
- **Reproducibility.** Prompts, protocols, an LLM-backbone study and a promised graph release are all provided. The graph resource could be useful in its own right.

## Weaknesses

**1. Possible leakage of benchmark-specific confounder knowledge through graph construction.** The confounding attributes of each benchmark are known in advance: sex, age, AP/PA projection, race, hospital, body site and colour. The Nuisance Modeling Agent adds "acquisition factors that may distort finding scores," and the case study shows an `AP-portable` nuisance node, which is exactly the NIH-pos confounder. Source-validation groups are also formed from the "nuisance reader whose source AUROC deviates most from 0.5." The paper needs to state clearly:
- whether the agents or prompts were told, directly or indirectly, about the benchmark confounders;
- whether graphs are per class or per dataset;
- how the nuisance vocabulary was decided.

If the nuisance nodes in effect name the confounder, much of the gain is closer to group-aware debiasing than to "knowledge-guided" robustness. In that case the right comparison is against methods that use the attribute (next point).

**2. Missing strong robustness baselines.** GroupDRO, JTT and DFR / last-layer retraining are cited but not compared. Neither is a simple attribute-aware baseline, such as group-balanced retraining or reweighting of a linear probe or KnoBo head using the nuisance-reader groups. GC-NCE already uses such groups for model selection, so these baselines are needed to separate the gain from graph-structured inference from the gain from worst-group-selected, nuisance-aware fitting. Without them, "best on all ten datasets" mostly means best among CBMs that ignore the confounder.

**3. ID performance drops, and the accuracy–robustness trade-off is not characterised.**
- Chest X-ray ID AUROC falls from about 95–98 to 89.1 (NIH-CheXpert ID is 84.6 versus about 100 for the baselines).
- A much smaller ∆ partly reflects a weaker source fit.
- Please report a Pareto-style view (ID versus OOD), or baselines selected with the same worst-group criterion. Baselines selected for average validation performance are naturally pushed toward the shortcut.

**4. The results depend heavily on the LLM backbone.** On chest X-ray, OOD AUROC ranges from 61.9 (GLM) to 78.5 (GPT-5.5), with NIH-pos ranging from 38.2 to 77.0. Each backbone has only one preparation trajectory, and the pipeline appears to have been developed with GPT-5.5. The seed std of ≤0.2 covers only head training and says nothing about variance in graph construction. Please report variance across multiple independent construction runs with the same LLM. Otherwise the headline numbers may reflect one favourable graph.

**5. Unexplained inconsistencies between tables.**
- Table 16 / Table 18: final-bank X-ray OOD AUROC is 72.6 with correction off and 75.3 with it on.
- Table 3: the same settings give 76.7 and 78.3.
- Appendix J says it uses "overall validation accuracy for checkpoint selection" instead of worst-group accuracy. A 3–4 point swing from the checkpoint-selection rule alone is large and should be discussed. It also suggests baselines would benefit from the same selection rule (see point 3).
- Table 13's uncorrected NIH-pos value (72.7) is also hard to reconcile with Table 16.

**6. Whether the graphs are clinically valid is not tested.** The graphs are claimed as a "reusable clinical evidence graph dataset," but no clinician reviewed them and no agreement with expert role assignments is reported. The compiler checks only that citations exist and match, not that the claims are medically correct. An expert audit, even on a sample of edges or roles, is needed to support the resource contribution and the interpretability claims. The interpretability claims are also supported only by one case study, with no user study or concept-intervention experiment.

**7. Limited scope and hand-set design choices.**
- All tasks are binary, and there are 14 class graphs in total. The scalability claims (mean-field approximation beyond 14 mechanisms, multi-class) are not tested empirically.
- Several thresholds are fixed by hand: 20 positive/negative annotations, 0.65 audit AUROC, 0.5 median split, λ_G = 1. Their sensitivity is not shown.
- The correction switch γ is binary per dataset. Its per-dataset benefit is noisy (Table 13), and the adaptive rule improves mean OOD by only 0.2 points (X-ray) and 0.7 points (skin) over the better fixed policy for each modality.

**8. Presentation.**
- The "Relative Gain (%)" rows are misleading. For example, +3074% on ISIC-sex ∆ comes from dividing by a near-zero denominator, and percentage gains on a gap metric are hard to read. Please use absolute point differences.
- The baseline count is inconsistent: "eight baselines" (Fig. 1), "twelve baselines" (Sec. 4.2), eleven listed in Table 1.
- The main tables lack standard deviations or significance tests.
- Typos: "existance," "Concequently," "CBMs aims," "annotates."

## Questions for the authors

1. What exactly did the Nuisance Modeling Agent see? Were benchmark attributes such as AP projection or hospital mentioned in any prompt, or chosen during development? Are graphs shared across all datasets of a modality?
2. How does GC-NCE compare with DFR / GroupDRO / JTT applied to a linear probe or KnoBo head, using the same nuisance-reader groups and worst-group model selection?
3. How do the baselines perform when their checkpoints are selected by source worst-group accuracy instead of average validation performance?
4. What is the variance of OOD AUROC across independent GPT-5.5 graph-construction runs?
5. Why do Table 3 and Tables 16–18 differ by 3–4 AUROC points for the same final bank?
6. Has a clinician validated any subset of the role assignments or mechanism–finding edges?
7. How are the noisy-OR strengths η and their "declared priors" obtained? Are they produced by the LLM?

## Assessment

- **Soundness:** 2 (fair). The evaluation is careful in places, but leakage of confounder knowledge, missing attribute-aware baselines and inconsistencies across tables leave the main claim open.
- **Presentation:** 3 (good). The writing is clear overall, but the notation is dense and the relative-gain metric is misleading.
- **Contribution:** 3 (good). The structured, role-typed knowledge head and graph resource are interesting, but the resource has not been checked against clinical judgement.
- **Rating: 5 (marginally below the acceptance threshold).**
- **Confidence:** 4.

The idea is novel and the empirical gains on the hardest splits are striking. Whether they come from clinical structure, or from graph-encoded knowledge of the confounder plus worst-group selection, is not yet settled. I would raise my score if the authors:
- clarify what the agents knew about the confounders;
- add attribute-aware robustness baselines with matched model selection;
- report variance across graph-construction runs;
- resolve the inconsistencies between tables.

---

The LLM-backbone variance, the Table 3 vs. Tables 16–18 discrepancy and the relative-gain issue are taken directly from the paper's own tables. Confounder leakage is a concern I inferred, not something the paper confirms, so I phrased it as a question for the authors. ICLR's reviewer policy asks you to disclose AI assistance, so edit this into your own words and judgement before submitting.

# ICLR 2027 Review: WebMCPWorld

**Paper:** *WebMCPWorld: Can LLMs Synthesize WebMCP Tools to Finish Open-Ended Tasks in Web Apps?* (submission 8BOmDcohc7)

I read the main paper (pp. 1–9) and Appendices A, B and the start of C (up to p. 20). I did not read the rest of the prompt appendix or Appendices D–E.

---

## Summary

The paper introduces WebMCPWorld, a benchmark for "tool synthesis." A model gets the source code of an existing open-source web application and a casual natural-language request. It must find the relevant functionality and write a WebMCP tool layer for it: JavaScript workflow functions with a declared parameter interface. Two tests then evaluate the generated artifact:

1. **Workflow execution test:** the workflow runs with ground-truth arguments.
2. **End-to-end agent test:** a fixed runtime agent (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash) receives the tool schemas and the user query and must complete the task.

The same model also judges the outcome. The benchmark covers 50 applications (50 to 3,159 kLOC), 258 features and 1,280 queries. The authors test 10 LLMs in 18 configurations across three harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, mini-swe-agent), with three repetitions each. Performance is very low:

- The best mean query-to-completion success rate (QCSR) is 10.0%, from Claude Code with Opus 5.
- A GUI-only baseline reaches 4.45%.
- 95% of feature–configuration–repetition groups have no agent-stage success.
- 62.4% of agent records fall into an "arguments not verifiably correct" category.

## Strengths

1. **Timely problem.** Turning existing web apps into agent-callable tool layers (WebMCP) is practically relevant. It is also clearly different from SWE-bench-style patching, whole-app generation, and tool use with tools that are already provided. The framing of the model as a "tool-maker for an existing app" is well motivated.
2. **Realistic, large-scale environments.** The 50 real, Dockerized, resettable applications include large codebases such as n8n, Twenty, Dolibarr and Medusa. The selection criteria (Appendix A) are sensible and clearly written, and the infrastructure is a substantial contribution in itself.
3. **Two-mode evaluation.** Separating "does the workflow work with correct inputs" from "can an agent use the tool to satisfy the request" is a good design idea in principle, because it tries to tell implementation errors apart from interface or usability errors.
4. **Unusually candid about limitations.** The paper repeatedly warns against over-reading comparisons: unequal budgets, non-nested denominators, and heuristic argument checks. The honesty is appreciated.
5. **Breadth of models and harnesses, with repetitions.** The authors report min, mean and max over three runs and give per-feature results (Table 6).

## Weaknesses

### 1. The synthesis budget probably decides the outcome, so the benchmark may mostly measure budget

The synthesis prompt (App. C.1.1, line 10) allows **at most 20 read steps and 30 steps in total** on repositories of up to 3 MLOC. A read step is any command such as `ls`, `cat` or `grep`. With so few steps, finding the right frontend handlers and API calls in Appsmith (1 MLOC) or n8n (3.2 MLOC), and then writing correct workflow code, is barely possible.

Several things suggest the low scores may say more about this budget than about whether models can do the task:

- The headline claim ("WebMCPWorld remains highly challenging … 10.0%") rests on this setting.
- The authors acknowledge that enforcement differs across harnesses: a hook for Claude Code, a command guard for mini, and prompt-only for Codex. Claude Code also counts subagent sessions separately and allows execution when its hook fails.
- So the best configuration may simply have had the most effective budget.

**Requested:** a budget-scaling study, for example 30, 100 and 300 steps on a subset, and a harness comparison with the budget held equal and enforced. Without these, neither the difficulty claim nor the ranking of configurations is interpretable.

### 2. Evaluation validity rests on a single, unvalidated LLM judge

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash is both the runtime agent and the judge. There is:

- no human agreement study for the judge,
- no second judge model,
- no check for bias toward artifacts that DeepSeek itself generated. The authors admit this is untested, and MSA–DeepSeek does lead on the workflow metric.

The paper also refers repeatedly to "revised" and "rejudged" labels (§3.4, §4.1, B.3) but does not describe the original judging procedure, what changed, or how many labels flipped. Post-hoc changes to the judge in a benchmark paper need full documentation.

Even the GUI-only baseline (4.45%) depends on this judge. A 60-step GUI agent scoring 0% on most features (Table 6) raises the question of whether the judge, the environment, or the agent is responsible.

**Requested:** human validation of a stratified sample of judge decisions, an agreement rate with a stronger judge, and a full account of the rejudging.

### 3. The fixed runtime agent confounds the end-to-end metric

Every end-to-end result goes through DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. A low ASR could therefore come from a bad tool or from a weak runtime agent failing to use a good tool. The authors acknowledge this (§5) but do not run the obvious control: re-running a subset of the synthesized artifacts with a stronger runtime agent.

That control matters because:

- the dominant failure category is "arguments not verifiably correct" (62.4%),
- "no workflow call" accounts for a further 17.4%,

and both read at least as much like runtime-agent failures as synthesis failures.

### 4. The metrics and denominators are confusing, and the main analysis category is uninformative

I had to re-read §4.1–4.2 several times to follow the numbers:

- There are four populations: 69,120 planned cells; 36,226 workflow-eligible cells; 34,924 agent-stage cells; and 31,266 cells "without complete mapping."
- The workflow-eligible and agent-stage sets are not nested.
- 5,177 records are excluded by a "pre-skip rule" that is never explained in the main text.
- Table 1 and Table 5 report different "Workflow" numbers under different denominators.

In addition, 31,266 of 69,120 cells lack complete reference-input mapping, about 45%. For almost half the benchmark, the authors' own pipeline cannot map ground-truth arguments onto the generated interface. That is a large part of the evaluation that cannot be checked.

The largest analysis category, "arguments not verifiably correct," is explicitly *not* an error category ("labels do not establish why a task failed"). As a result, the analysis section offers little diagnostic insight.

**Requested:** a single clear evaluation flowchart with every exclusion rule, a reduced metric set, and a human-annotated failure taxonomy on a sample.

### 5. The task definition is underspecified on reusability

The title and abstract stress *reusable* tools, but synthesis receives only "the first query of each feature" (C.1). Reuse is then judged on other query variants that the model never saw.

That is a reasonable generalization test, but the benchmark gives no specification of what interface is expected. Reference schemas are deliberately withheld. A model therefore has to guess the parameterization, and a reasonable interface that differs from the reference can fail the mapping step. It is unclear whether failures here reflect a lack of capability or ambiguity in the task.

The paper should also show inter-annotator or reference-solution evidence that each task can be solved within the given constraints. In particular, it should report whether a human or oracle produced a passing WebMCP tool for every feature.

### 6. Unclear difficulty signal and solvability

- Difficulty measured by GUI steps does not predict success (Table 3, Fig. 5), so the paper offers no validated difficulty structure.
- Many features show 0.0 for all metrics across all 18 configurations (Table 6).
- The benchmark does not show that these tasks are solvable. A reference WebMCP implementation per feature, even for a subset, would establish an upper bound and confirm that the harness and the judge can award a pass.

### 7. Presentation

The writing is dense and hedged to the point of hiding the key messages. Many sentences in §4 are disclaimers. Specific problems:

- **Figure 2 has internal inconsistencies:**
  - The workflow test reports `conversation_id=1241`, but the judge reads conversation `#2428`.
  - "88 steps · 7.2 s" for a single workflow execution needs explaining.
- **Feature counts don't match.** Table 6 covers 257 of 258 features, and the missing one is not identified.
- **Jargon goes undefined in the main text,** including "pre-skip rule," "eligibility rules," "retained," "corrected ledger" and "runtime self-reports."
- **The contribution list is thin.** The third bullet ("evaluation results and analysis") does not state any insight.

### 8. Contamination

All 50 applications are popular open-source GitHub repositories (>50 stars, many very popular), so pretraining exposure is likely. The authors acknowledge this but offer no mitigation, such as a held-out private app or obfuscated variants.

## Questions for the Authors

1. How do results change if the synthesis budget is raised to, for example, 100 or 300 steps with equal enforcement across harnesses?
2. What is the human–judge agreement rate? What exactly did "revised/rejudged" labeling change, and how many labels flipped?
3. Do the end-to-end results change materially if the runtime agent is replaced with a stronger model, for example Opus 5, while the artifacts stay fixed?
4. What is the "pre-skip rule" that removes 5,177 measurements?
5. Why do 45% of cells lack complete reference-input mapping, and is this a property of the models or of the mapping procedure?
6. Is there a reference (human- or oracle-written) WebMCP tool for each feature showing that it passes the pipeline?
7. Why does the GUI-only baseline score 0% on the large majority of features even though these features were originally explored and recorded by a GUI agent during construction (§3.1)?
8. Please explain the ID mismatch in Figure 2 (1241 vs. #2428).

## Minor Comments

- §4.1: "nominal `--max-steps=50` setting is not enforced by the CLI." The text should state up front which budget each harness actually ran under.
- Table 1 mixes conditional (Workflow, ASR) and unconditional (QCSR) metrics in adjacent columns. Separating them visually, or moving the conditional metrics to the appendix, would help.
- Figure 5 (right) needs axis labels with units, and its text is partly obscured.
- The abstract says "1280 colloquial user queries." Some description of how the query variants were generated (LLM vs. human) and validated belongs in the main text.
- The AI use statement says generative AI assisted in dataset preparation, GUI exploration and query generation. The degree of human verification of queries and expected states should be quantified.

## Overall Assessment

The problem is new and important, and the environment infrastructure (50 resettable real-world apps) could be valuable to the community. In its current form, however, the paper does not show that its headline numbers measure the intended capability. Four issues each push the reported performance down in ways the benchmark cannot tell apart from a lack of model capability:

- a very tight synthesis budget, enforced differently across harnesses;
- a single, unvalidated LLM judge that is also the runtime agent;
- about 45% of cells that cannot be fully verified;
- no evidence that the tasks can be solved.

The analysis mostly lists accounting categories rather than giving insight into why models fail. I would expect a substantially stronger paper after adding budget scaling, judge validation, a runtime-agent ablation, reference solutions, and a simpler metric presentation.

|---|---|
| **Soundness** | 2 (fair) |
| **Presentation** | 2 (fair) |
| **Contribution** | 2 (fair) |
| **Rating** | **4: marginally below the acceptance threshold** (leaning 3 if judge/budget concerns are not addressed) |
| **Confidence** | 4: confident, but I did not read every part of the appendix (D–E, full prompts) in detail |

# Review: PINN-ffusion: Physics-Informed Neural Network via Diffusion-based Adaptive Sampling and Anisotropic Domain Decomposition

## Summary

The paper builds on PINN-ball (Bonfanti et al., NeurIPS 2025), which couples adversarial adaptive sampling with dynamic ball-shaped domain decomposition and trains with second-order (LM) optimization. It makes two changes:

1. **Diffusion-based sampling.** The minimax sampler is replaced by an explicit density. The initial density is p₀ ∝ r², the squared residual (RAD-style). It is smoothed by the Neumann heat kernel for a time *t*, and samples are moved with the corresponding probability-flow ODE. Because the heat kernel is strictly positive, the density stays bounded below. The authors use this to prove that driving the weighted loss to zero also drives the L² residual to zero (Thm 3.1).
2. **Anisotropic decomposition.** The isotropic RBF balls become ellipsoids defined by a Mahalanobis metric G. G mixes a covariance-based "diversity" term with a trace-normalized outer product of residual gradients (an "uncertainty" term). Thm 3.3 restates the classical anisotropic interpolation argument (h_i ∝ 1/g_i beats isotropic cells).

The authors also approximate LM with Truncated Newton (Prop. 5.1). Experiments cover five standard benchmarks: Helmholtz, Burgers, Klein–Gordon, Boussinesq–Burgers and Navier–Stokes (cylinder wake). PINN-ffusion has the lowest mean error on all of them. There is a 2×2 ablation on Navier–Stokes, comparisons against RAD and QR-DEIM sampling, sensitivity tables and a cost table.

## Strengths

- **The weaknesses targeted are real.** The adversarial sampler needs regularization, and isotropic balls are a poor fit for thin layers. Replacing a learned sampler with a closed-form, parameter-free density is simpler and slightly cheaper (Table 14: 36.5 s vs 45.2 s per epoch, 36 GB vs 38 GB).
- **The anisotropic metric is reasonable and easy to understand.** Using the outer product of ∇(r²) avoids cancellation across a layer, and trace normalization keeps the shape independent of residual magnitude. The Burgers and Helmholtz figures (Figs. 3 and 7) show ellipses aligning with the structures they are meant to follow.
- **The empirical package is fairly complete for a PINN paper.** It has 10 seeds, medians and IQRs, a component ablation, sampler swaps against RAD and QR-DEIM, hyperparameter sensitivity, matched parameter counts and released code.
- **The ablation suggests the two components are complementary** on Navier–Stokes, especially for pressure.

## Weaknesses

**1. The "diffusion" framing overstates what the method is, and may hide that it is close to uniform sampling.**
- No score network is learned and no generative model is involved. The method takes a residual-proportional density (exactly RAD's p ∝ r^k/E[r^k] with c = 0), convolves it with a reflecting heat kernel, and samples from the result.
- Sampling from this density is just "sample from p₀, then add reflected Gaussian noise of variance 2t." The probability-flow ODE produces the same marginal and seems unnecessary. It also still needs samples from p₀, and the paper does not say how p₀ is sampled in multiple dimensions (resampling from a candidate pool?).
- The citations to DDIM and score-based models are window dressing. Section 2.2 on DDIM is not used anywhere in the method.
- The scale of *t* is a serious concern. With κ = 1, the first non-trivial mode decays as exp(−π²t/L²). For the default t = 20 on a unit-length axis (Helmholtz on [0,1]², and the x-range of Klein–Gordon), that is about e^{−197}: the density is numerically uniform. For Navier–Stokes, the spatial axes give roughly e^{−4} to e^{−12}.
- Either the coordinates or *t* are rescaled in a way the paper does not describe, or the "adaptive" sampler is close to uniform on several benchmarks. Please state the effective smoothing length √(2t) relative to each domain axis, for every benchmark. Please also plot the sampling density actually used.

**2. Theorem 3.1 is close to trivial and does not separate this method from simpler ones.**
- Any sampling density bounded below by m > 0 satisfies J ≥ m‖r‖². This holds for uniform sampling, RAD with c > 0, or any mixture with a uniform component. The heat kernel adds nothing beyond positivity.
- The "no collapse" property is therefore not a distinguishing contribution. RAD with c > 0 already has it, and so does a simple mixture with uniform.
- The bound is also very loose: m(t) is exponentially small for small t, and the optimum t (≈20) is the regime where m(t) ≈ 1/|Ω|, i.e., nearly uniform.
- The theorem also concerns the population integral, while training uses a finite sample of N points. A statement about sampling error, or about training dynamics, would be more informative.

**3. Theorem 3.3 is a classical result that is only loosely tied to the method.**
- The h_i ∝ g_i⁻¹ argument via AM-GM is standard in anisotropic meshing (Formaggia & Perotto; Huang). It applies to a best-case piecewise interpolation bound, not to a partition-of-unity mixture of neural networks trained by a non-convex optimizer.
- The constructed G does not implement h ∝ 1/g. Its eigenvalues are capped at 1+ξ, and it is mixed with a covariance term.
- The theorem bounds an upper bound, yet the text says "E² is minimized." Φ and Φ² are also used inconsistently in the proof (Eqs. 53–55).
- Proposition 5.1 (CG converges to the solution of an SPD system) is textbook material and does not need to be a proposition.

**4. The experimental comparison is confounded by the optimizer.**
- PINN, XPINN and APINN are run "with their original training settings" (first-order). PINN-ball and PINN-ffusion use 2,000 second-order TN/LM iterations. The 2–5 orders-of-magnitude gaps in Table 2 against first-order baselines therefore mostly reflect the optimizer, not the contributions.
- The only controlled comparison is against PINN-ball. Missing controls:
  - a single PINN with TN/LM plus RAD sampling;
  - FBPINN, which is listed in Table 1 but not evaluated;
  - stronger modern baselines such as PirateNets, R3 sampling, and causal or self-adaptive weighting.
- Please also report whether your PINN-ball numbers match those in Bonfanti et al.

**5. The statistical claims are weaker than stated.**
- "Lowest error on every benchmark" is not supported where the standard deviations overlap or exceed the gap. Examples:
  - Helmholtz: 1.28e−9 ± 1.86e−9 vs 1.51e−9 ± 1.72e−9;
  - Klein–Gordon: std 2.07e−5 > mean 1.11e−5;
  - Boussinesq v: 8.99e−2 vs 1.15e−1 with large std.
- The Wilcoxon test on eight paired IQRs (several are components of the same PDE, so not independent) is an unusual way to show robustness.
- The ablation, sampler comparison and sensitivity analysis all use Navier–Stokes only. At least Burgers and Klein–Gordon should be included, since the anisotropy argument is made mainly with Burgers.

**6. Inconsistencies in reported results that need checking.**
- Table 10 (sensitivity to the stability constant) repeats the v and p columns of Table 9 (sensitivity to ξ) digit for digit: 5.88e−3 / 5.82e−3 / 5.87e−3 / 5.98e−3 and 1.19e−2 / 1.18e−2 / 1.26e−2 / 1.29e−2. This looks like a copy-paste error and needs correcting.
- Table 11 lists t ∈ {10, 20, 50, 80} but has five rows, and the text mentions t = 100.
- Eq. 15 uses d²/s_j, while Algorithm 5 uses /s²_{k,j}.
- Eq. 12 and Algorithm 5 line 11 give different formulas for G (an extra α_k I).
- How the heat-kernel series is truncated, and how s_{k,j} is updated (Alg. 5 line 12), are not specified.

**7. Scope and cost.**
- All benchmarks are classic low-dimensional Raissi-repository problems. None has a genuine thin boundary layer or interface, apart from Burgers' shock, even though the paper motivates the method with such problems. A convection-dominated or high-Péclet problem, or a 3D case, would test the anisotropy claim much better.
- The method needs about 36 GB and 36 s per epoch for a roughly 5k-parameter model. This limits practicality, and accuracy-versus-wall-clock against first-order methods is not reported.
- The "O(dN)" cost claim for Eq. 45 ignores that evaluating p(x, t) requires an integral against p₀, which costs at least O(N²) with an empirical p₀ or O(N · n_modes) with a truncated series.

**8. Presentation.**
- Notation is sloppy. For example, after Eq. 1, f and h are called "predicted residual points" and "predicted boundary points."
- Several citations look irrelevant to the claims they support: Grill et al. and Travis & Ray for diffusion models, Kostic et al. and Qian et al. for a zero eigenvalue, Liu et al. (KSD) for Fubini's theorem.
- Typos: "Framewsorks", "Newmann", "Lagenberg", "postivie", "innter", "intergers", "spatitemporal".
- Table 1 is hard to parse.

## Questions for the authors

1. What is the effective smoothing scale √(2t) relative to each axis of each benchmark? Are the coordinates normalized? Please show the actual p_{t,k} for Helmholtz, where t = 20 on [0,1]² appears to give a uniform density.
2. How do you sample from p₀ ∝ r² in 2D and 3D? Given that, what does the probability-flow ODE add over simply adding reflected Gaussian noise?
3. How does PINN-ffusion compare with (a) a single network trained by TN with RAD sampling, and (b) PINN-ball with RAD sampling replacing its adversarial sampler? These isolate the "no minimax" benefit.
4. Can you report Table 2 for XPINN and APINN trained with the same TN/LM optimizer and budget?
5. Please confirm whether Tables 9 and 10 are duplicated by mistake, and give the correct numbers.
6. Do your PINN-ball results reproduce those in Bonfanti et al. (2025) on the shared benchmarks?
7. What happens on a problem with a genuinely thin anisotropic layer, such as a convection–diffusion boundary layer with ε ≪ 1?

## Soundness / Presentation / Contribution
- **Soundness:** 2 (fair). The theorems are correct but near-trivial or loosely connected to the method, the t-scaling question is open, the baselines are confounded by the optimizer, and some tables are inconsistent.
- **Presentation:** 2 (fair).
- **Contribution:** 2 (fair). These are incremental changes to PINN-ball. The sampler is essentially RAD plus heat-kernel smoothing, and the anisotropic metric is a sensible but modest extension.

## Overall recommendation
**Rating: 4 (marginally below the acceptance threshold) → leaning 3 (reject).** I'm open to raising it if the questions above are answered convincingly.

The paper addresses real limitations of PINN-ball, and the anisotropic decomposition is a reasonable idea backed by some visual evidence. But the diffusion component is mostly a re-labeling of residual-based sampling with Gaussian smoothing, and on several benchmarks it may be nearly uniform. The theoretical results add little beyond positivity of the sampling density and a classical meshing inequality. The main empirical gains are confounded by the optimizer, or fall within seed variance on several benchmarks. Experiments restricted to one benchmark for ablations, plus duplicated sensitivity tables, further weaken confidence.

**Confidence:** 4 (confident, but I didn't check every detail of the code or the appendix figures).

# ICLR 2027 Review: *Intrinsic Wasserstein Rates for Score-Based Diffusion Models on Smooth Manifolds*

## Summary

The paper studies score-based diffusion models when the data distribution $P_0$ lives on a compact $d$-dimensional $C^\infty$ submanifold $\mathcal M\subset[0,1]^D$ with positive reach, and has a $\beta$-Hölder density bounded away from zero. The estimator works interval by interval. On each time slab, it approximately minimises the denoising score-matching loss over a class of sparse ReLU networks that take ambient inputs, with fixed input truncation and output clipping. It is not given estimated tangent spaces, anchors or coordinates.

The main result (Theorem 2.2 / Corollary H.2), for $d>2$, is
$\mathbb E\,W_1(P_0,\widehat P^{\rm box}_{t_0}) \lesssim_{\log} D^{O_\beta(d)}\, n^{-(\beta+1)/(d+2\beta)}$.
This holds for the early-stopped continuous-time reverse SDE, followed by projection onto the cube.

The proof builds two kinds of comparison networks:
- **Moderate and high noise:** tangent-cell local Gaussian-moment approximations.
- **Low noise:** a "projection-centred Laplace" construction. It first factors out the common normal Gaussian term $e^{-\|r\|^2/2\sigma_t^2}$, so the denominator $\bar Q$ has a polynomial lower bound. It then implements the nearest-point projection through finite-anchor Gauss–Newton iterations in chart coordinates.

These feed into an oracle inequality and a reverse-SDE perturbation argument. Corollary H.14 gives a discretised exponential-integrator version. The appendix is roughly 100 pages of proofs.

## Strengths

1. **Clear question.** Can plain ambient ERM over score networks reach the intrinsic minimax $W_1$ exponent without a manifold-estimation step? This matters for theory that wants to explain why diffusion models adapt to low-dimensional structure.
2. **Good handling of the low-noise singularity.** Factoring out the normal Gaussian term before approximating the ratio $\mathcal U/\mathcal Q$ is a clean idea. It explains why a noise-scale tangent cover (about $\sigma_{t_0}^{-d}$ cells) is not needed. The Gauss–Newton projection module with explicit $D$ dependence is a reusable technical piece.
3. **Rate matches the benchmark.** The exponent $(\beta+1)/(d+2\beta)$ equals the Niles-Weed & Berthet minimax rate for lower-bounded densities on $d$-dimensional domains.
4. **Careful and honest writing.** Section 5 explains clearly why the slower small-noise score rate still gives the target distribution rate (via $\sqrt{t_1}$). The authors also state openly what they do *not* improve (lines 087–089, A.2).
5. **Discretisation is covered.** A finite-step sampler counterpart with a score-evaluation count is included.

## Weaknesses

1. **Limited novelty relative to prior work, by the authors' own account.**
   - Tang & Yang (2024) already obtain the same intrinsic $W_1$ exponent "without explicitly estimating the manifold" (line 078).
   - Azangulov et al. (v3) obtain the same exponent with *no* explicit $D$ factor.
   - The paper states that its differences "concern the construction and estimator interface, not a new sample-size exponent or an improved ambient prefactor."

   So the contribution is mainly a different proof route and estimator interface. The main text does not say precisely what Tang & Yang's estimator interface is, or why the present one is meaningfully different. If Tang & Yang also use ambient-network ERM, the paper's headline question was already answered. Appendix A covers Zhang et al. and Azangulov et al., but gives Tang & Yang no comparable treatment. This is the most important gap to close.

2. **The ambient dependence is weak in practice.** The factor $D^{O_\beta(d)}$ is called "polynomial," but its exponent grows with $d$ and with $\beta$ (through $q_{\rm geom}\ge 6\beta+4$ and related constants). For realistic $d$, this can be far worse than the full-dimensional rates the paper aims to improve on. It is also strictly worse than Azangulov et al.'s dimension-free factor. The main text should make $O_\beta(d)$ explicit, or at least give its order, and discuss in which regime of $(n,D,d)$ the bound beats ambient-dimension results. The same applies to the hidden $\Gamma^{C}_{\mathcal M,q}$ and $p_{\min}^{-C}$ powers.

3. **The estimator is idealised.**
   - The expectations over diffusion time and Gaussian corruption are taken exactly (lines 381–383). Monte Carlo error is excluded.
   - The optimisation excess $\mathcal E_{{\rm opt},k}$ is simply assumed small, at the rate $\varepsilon_n$.
   - The estimator needs $d$, $\beta$ and the geometry and density bounds in order to set $t_0$, $t_1$, the cell radii and the architecture sizes.
   - The learned score is a collection of separate networks, one per interval, rather than one time-conditioned network.

   Each of these departs from how diffusion models are trained. Together, they weaken the claim that this explains practical ambient training. Sampling over $t$ and $x_t$ is a standard part of DSM. Its omission could be handled with a standard concentration argument and should be at least sketched. Adaptivity to unknown $d$ and $\beta$ is not discussed.

4. **Restricted to $d>2$.** The simplified theorem needs $d>2$, both for $n^{-1/2}\lesssim\varepsilon_n$ and for a finite $q_\star$. The $d=2$ case only gets a logarithmic remark, and $d=1$ is not covered. A short discussion of what fails for $d\le2$ would help.

5. **Strong regularity assumptions.**
   - A $C^\infty$ manifold is assumed "for convenience." The proof actually uses a finite-order envelope $\Gamma_{\mathcal M,q_{\rm geom}}$ with $q_{\rm geom}\ge\max\{6\beta+4,\ 2+3(\beta+1)\}$. That is far more geometric smoothness than the $\beta$ needed for the density, and it is not compared with what prior work requires (e.g. $C^{\beta+1}$ manifolds).
   - The "small-noise reach conditions" (236)–(237) and the requirement $D\vee p_{\min}^{-1}\le n^{a_0}$ are deferred to the appendix. Their content should appear in the main text.

6. **Hard to verify at conference scale.** The correctness rests on roughly 100 pages of appendix with many interacting constants: $C_\varrho$, $c_{\rm cap}$, $C_\star$, $c_T$, $a_0$, $q_\star$. A reviewer cannot check this fully in an ICLR cycle. In addition, the main text relies heavily on informal statements written with $\lesssim_{\log}$ and $\Gamma^C$. A dependency diagram of the key lemmas, plus a one-page proof sketch of the low-noise construction (the genuinely new part), would make the work much easier to audit. A journal (AoS/JMLR/Bernoulli) may suit this level of detail better.

7. **No numerical illustration.** No experiments are expected for a theory paper. Still, even a small synthetic check would make the central mechanism concrete: for example, whether ambient DSM-trained networks show the predicted low-noise behaviour on a curved manifold such as a torus in $\mathbb R^D$ with varying $D$.

8. **Presentation.** Parts of the main text read as long chains of qualifications ("under the stated geometry, regularity, and optimization conditions…"). The final projection $\mathrm{Proj}_{[0,1]^D}$ to the cube is a convenience that should be stated plainly in the theorem. Listing $D^{O_\beta(d)}$ alongside $\Gamma$ and $p_{\min}$ in one table against Oko et al., Chen et al., Tang & Yang, Azangulov et al. and Zhang et al. would make the positioning much clearer than the current prose.

## Questions for the authors

1. What exactly separates your estimator from Tang & Yang (2024)? Do they also run ambient ERM without data-dependent preprocessing? If so, what does this paper add beyond an alternative proof?
2. What is $O_\beta(d)$ explicitly? For example, what is the $D$ exponent for $\beta=1$, $d=5$? For which $(n,D,d)$ does your bound improve on ambient-dimension rates such as Oko et al.?
3. Can the exact-expectation assumption be removed by sampling $t$ and noise, and at what cost to the rate?
4. Can the result be made adaptive to unknown $d$ and $\beta$, for example through model selection over the cutoff schedule?
5. Is the geometric order $q_{\rm geom}\gtrsim 6\beta$ essential to your construction, or an artefact of it? What breaks with a $C^{\beta+1}$ manifold?
6. Would a single time-conditioned network (shared parameters) keep the guarantee?
7. Is the nearest-point projection actually needed in the low-noise construction? Or would any centring map with controlled normal residual suffice?

## Overall assessment

This is a technically serious and carefully written theory paper. Its low-noise Gaussian-factor-removal construction is a nice idea. However, the headline rate is already known (Tang & Yang 2024; Azangulov et al.). The ambient prefactor $D^{O_\beta(d)}$ is worse than the best existing result. The estimator is idealised in ways that narrow its relevance to practice. The paper's own framing ("not a new sample-size exponent or an improved ambient prefactor") leaves the contribution resting on the construction and the estimator interface. That is not clearly enough separated from prior work to clear the bar, and the size of the appendix makes verification within the review cycle impractical.

- **Soundness:** 3 / 4 (appears careful; not fully verified)
- **Presentation:** 2 / 4
- **Contribution:** 2 / 4
- **Rating:** 5 (marginally below the acceptance threshold)
- **Confidence:** 3. I read the main text and the related-work appendix but did not check the roughly 100 pages of proofs.

# Review: I-OctoScene: Multi-Agent 3D Scene Synthesis with Multimodal Interactive Instructions

## Summary

The paper presents I-OctoScene, an LLM/VLM agent framework for building indoor 3D scenes over several rounds. It splits the single-agent loop of SceneWeaver into four roles: Art Director/Consultant, Interior Designer, Engineer and Quality Inspector. It adds two components:

- **PMIR** lets an external "Instructor" give feedback each round as text, as structured click/select JSON, or as marks drawn on a gridded top-down render. The Instructor can be a VLM ("Ours") or a human ("Ours†").
- **IATC** adds "Adaptive Tooling Skills" (ATSs). These are fixed multi-step tool recipes, each described by a "Skill Manual" (trigger rules, procedure, suitable tools, targets). Three are given: FillEmptyArea, ReplaceAsset and SurfaceDecoration.

The paper also proposes an "Interaction Evaluation Benchmark", a 10-point score made of GPT-judged quality (4 pts), interaction diversity (2 pts), per-round adherence (2 pts) and final query fulfillment (2 pts). Experiments cover bedroom and living room scenes plus 8 open-vocabulary room types, scored with GPT-4.1, along with a 10-user human study.

## Strengths

1. **Useful goal.** Interactive, step-by-step control of agentic scene synthesis is practically relevant. Combining language, clicks and drawn marks on a gridded render is a reasonable, low-cost way to ground user intent spatially.
2. **Clear system description.** Prompts, the tool list, the ATS definitions, the scene representation and the pipeline (Alg. 1) are documented in the appendix, which helps reproducibility.
3. **Broad qualitative coverage.** There are many room types and step-by-step visualizations (Figs. 4, 10–13, 19–24), and the figures showing tool calls with their arguments make the system's behavior easy to inspect.
4. **Cost reporting.** Time and token costs per round (Tables 6–7) are a welcome addition.

## Weaknesses

### 1. The evaluation is circular and likely inflated (major)

- **The agent optimizes the evaluator.** The Quality Inspector's prompt (App. B.2) is the same Real./Func./Lay./Comp. rubric used as the evaluation metric. App. C says of the quality component: "See the agent prompts above". Both run on GPT-4.1 (App. D). So each round the system optimizes the exact GPT-4.1 judge it is later scored by, and the VLM Instructor is probably the same model as well. The rubric even rewards specific things ("each shelf is full of objects (>5)", "empty area < 50%") that FillEmptyArea and SurfaceDecoration are built to produce. Higher Comp./#Obj scores are therefore not independent evidence of better scenes. A held-out judge is needed: a different model family, a different rubric, or human raters blind to the method on all settings.
- **The "Int." benchmark is designed in the method's favor.** The 2-point "Diversity" component is assigned by rule: 2 points for human feedback, 1 for LLM feedback, 0 for none (App. C). It measures which features a system supports, not how well it performs, and it alone builds in a gap between Ours and Ours†. Int. is reported only for the proposed method; every baseline shows "–". So the headline benchmark offers no comparison at all.
- **The judge prompts tell the judge to be lenient.** The per-round adherence prompt says "Be very lenient and flexible! If a new object is present vaguely corresponding to the request, assume it correct". The fulfillment prompt says "Be lenient". The fulfillment step also first compresses all demands into 1–2 sentences while "ignoring ... coordinate positions". This removes exactly the spatial precision that PMIR claims to provide. Under these prompts, the ~8.2–9.6 Int. scores tell us little about whether instructions were followed.

### 2. The comparisons are unequal

- "Ours†" gets human corrective feedback every round. ATISS, DiffuScene, PhyScene, LayoutGPT, Holodeck and I-Design get none, and SceneWeaver gets only self-reflection. Beating non-interactive baselines with a human in the loop is expected, not a finding. The fair control is SceneWeaver, or a single agent using the same tools, given the same external instructions over the same number of rounds and with the same LLM-call budget. This control is especially missing from Fig. 5(a), which compares round-by-round gains against SceneWeaver.
- Most baseline numbers are copied from SceneWeaver (App. D), while SceneWeaver and I-OctoScene are re-run "under unified settings" that are not specified. Mixing copied and re-run results makes the comparisons hard to interpret.
- The amount and type of human feedback for Ours† is not reported: number of users, instructions per round, expertise, or whether the authors themselves acted as instructors.

### 3. The results do not support "state-of-the-art" claims as strongly as stated

- In Table 1, Holodeck matches or beats Ours on several cells: bedroom Lay. 7.8 vs. 7.5, living room Comp. 8.1 vs. 8.0 and Lay. 7.6 vs. 7.6. In Table 2, several open-vocabulary cells are ties or losses (e.g., bathroom Func., restaurant). Gains over SceneWeaver are usually 0.3–0.7 on a 10-point LLM-judged scale.
- Open-vocabulary results average only 3 runs, and ablations also use 3. No standard deviations, confidence intervals or significance tests are reported, so many differences may be noise.
- #OB = #CN = 0 is inherited from SceneWeaver's physics-aware tools and does not set this method apart.
- The ablation (Table 3) is hard to read. The "Ours" row (21.0 objects) does not match Table 1 (20.3 or 21.7). "w/o User" produces more objects (24.3) and the same Comp. (8.0), which is not explained. "w/o Multi-Agent" is not specified: does it get the same prompts, tools, rounds and Instructor feedback? It is also unclear whether ablating PMIR removes the VLM Instructor or the human.

### 4. Limited technical novelty

- **The multi-agent split** separates one prompt into four role prompts that share one context and one model (App. B.2). The claimed problem, "coupling bias" in single agents, is never defined or measured. The only evidence is one ablation row, which also changes the amount of computation spent.
- **ATSs** are hand-written macros: two-step or one-step fixed sequences over existing SceneWeaver tools, selected by a natural-language trigger. SurfaceDecoration is a single call to AddCrowd. The object-oriented-programming and cognitive-hierarchical-planning framing overstates what is three prompt-level templates. Nothing is "adaptive" beyond the LLM filling in arguments, and there is no analysis of trigger accuracy, of failures, or of scaling to more skills.
- **PMIR's** visual instructions amount to drawing a red box on the render and asking GPT-4.1 to estimate its coordinates. The accuracy of this grounding (red box → 3D target) is never measured, though it is the key technical claim behind multimodal interaction.

Overall, the contribution reads as careful engineering on top of SceneWeaver more than a research contribution at ICLR's bar.

### 5. Practicality and cost

A round takes 4–15 minutes and a scene about 1 hour (Table 6). That is long for an "interactive" system, and SceneWeaver's cost is not reported for comparison. Claiming that this beats human designers who need "several hours" is not supported by any measurement.

### 6. Ethics and presentation issues

- The ethics statement (App. F) says there are "no human-subject studies". The paper does include a 10-user human evaluation (App. E.1) and human-in-the-loop instructors. This contradiction should be fixed, with consent/IRB status and participant recruitment described.
- There are presentation errors:
  - A sentence about evaluation is misplaced in the method paragraph of the Introduction (l. 93).
  - E.5 says "we can observe that:" and then gives nothing.
  - The input is called E_i in Eq. 3 but I_i in Alg. 1.
  - The text switches between "Art Director" and "Art Consultant".
  - The "rollback mechanism" appears only in the appendix.
  - "Childred room" (Fig. 8).
  - Calling the collection "multimodal" when the control instruction is just JSON converted to text.
  - The human-study questionnaire description is placed oddly in App. D.

## Questions for the authors

1. Can you re-evaluate with a judge that the agents never see, for example a different VLM family and/or blind human ratings on all room types, and report how scores change?
2. Can you run SceneWeaver, and your "w/o Multi-Agent" variant, with the *same* VLM/human instructions, round count and token budget, and report the results?
3. How accurate is spatial grounding from visual and control instructions (e.g., error between the intended region and the placed object position)? Was any instruction followed with a strict rather than lenient judge?
4. Who were the human instructors and evaluators? Were they blind to the method, how many instructions did they give, and how was inter-rater agreement measured?
5. How often are ATSs triggered correctly, and how do results change with ATSs removed but the same tools kept?
6. Please report standard deviations and number of runs for every table entry.

## Rating

- **Soundness:** 2 (fair). The evaluation is circular and the comparisons are uncontrolled.
- **Presentation:** 2 (fair)
- **Contribution:** 2 (fair)
- **Overall:** 3 (reject, not good enough)
- **Confidence:** 4

**Justification.** Interactive multimodal control of agentic scene synthesis is a worthwhile direction, and the system is documented in detail. However, the core evidence rests on a GPT-4.1 judge that the system itself optimizes against, plus an interaction benchmark that rewards supported features and tells its judge to be lenient. Key comparisons give the proposed method external or human feedback that the baselines don't receive. The technical additions (role-split prompts and three hand-written tool macros) are modest. I would reconsider with independent evaluation, interaction-matched baselines and a measured analysis of grounding accuracy.
